system:
You are a senior SOC analyst investigating Kubernetes activity. Work only from evidence returned by your tools; never invent event IDs, IPs or principals.

Scope: one day (2026-10-14) of Kubernetes API audit logs for the payments-prod cluster, which runs on AWS (EKS), GCP (GKE) and Azure (AKS).

Data: ocsf_enriched holds all three clouds normalized to the OCSF API Activity schema (one row per audit event; metadata.uid is the audit event ID), with context already joined onto every row in the `enrichment` struct: the person behind each principal (name, department, out-of-office, usual client OS and mismatch), service-account ownership and whether it called from outside its expected network, source IP reputation, asset classification, and for pod creates whether the workload is privileged, platform-allowlisted and from an approved registry. Tools search and summarize it directly; query_sql is available for anything else.

Method: start broad, form hypotheses, verify each against the data, and check enrichment context before concluding. Cite every malicious event you rely on by its audit event ID. When finished, call submit_verdict exactly once; the investigation ends when you do.

input.summary: Jordan Doe's (jdoe@example.com, Payments Engineering) credentials were stolen and used from 198.51.100.23. That IP is rated malicious: NIGHTOWL-HOSTING, NL, bulletproof hosting, runs an open Docker registry on :5000 and is tagged for K8s API brute-forcing. Jordan is on PTO (Oct 12-19), and the linux kubectl client doesn't match the darwin machine he normally uses. The same scripted attack ran against all three payments-prod clusters in turn: EKS 14:02-14:25, GKE 14:38-15:01, AKS 15:11-15:34. In each cluster the actor checked their own permissions and listed namespaces. Reads of kube-system secrets and a kube-system job create were denied. They then read payments/payments-db-credentials, created a privileged pod (hostPID, host root filesystem mounted, not allowlisted) called debug-tools-7f9c, and exec'd into it. From that pod they evidently took the cluster-admin argocd-application-controller service-account token, then used it from the same external IP (flagged outside its expected network) to create the ClusterRoleBinding jdoe-break-glass, which gives jdoe cluster-admin. With that they set up persistence: a kube-system DaemonSet kube-metrics-agent and a CronJob node-cert-rotate, both pulling images from 198.51.100.23:5000, plus a NodePort service metrics-agent-np on port 30080 in default. Last, they listed secrets across all namespaces (the alert). Nothing else from the attacker IP, and no activity on the attacker-created resources from any other IP, appears in the logs.

That IP is rated malicious: NIGHTOWL-HOSTING, NL, bulletproof hosting, runs an open Docker registry on :5000 and is tagged for K8s API brute-forcing.
